article_title: Competency-Based Education in College Settings
citation: Ann Person. (2016). Competency-Based Education in College Settings. Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: CBE curriculum development was more collaborative and consistent than in traditional programs, relying on instructional designers and standardization tools
description: The evaluation found that CBE curriculum development differed from traditional program development: it "was more collaborative and consistent than in traditional programs and relied on instructional designers and tools to support standardization." This design pattern pairs faculty collaboration with dedicated instructional design staff and shared tools so that competencies, assessments, and course materials are consistent across a program. The brief reports this as a distinguishing implementation feature of the consortium's CBE programs.
requirements: Instructional designers and standardization tools to support consistent curriculum
Collaboration among curriculum developers
target_learning_goals: job-aligned competencies delivered through standardized curricula
examples: The consortium relied on instructional designers and tools to support standardization of CBE curricula, per the evaluation's key findings

article_title: Implementation and Outcomes of Competency-Based Education in Three Community Colleges: Findings from the Comprehensive Evaluation of a TAACCCT Grant (Executive Summary)
citation: Person, A. E., Thomas, J., & Goble, L. (2016). Implementation and Outcomes of Competency-Based Education in Three Community Colleges: Findings from the Comprehensive Evaluation of a TAACCCT Grant (Executive Summary). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Offer competency-based education models as one of multiple options, since they appear best suited for mature, academically well-prepared students
description: Based on the evaluation, the authors recommend that "CBE models should be one of multiple options for college students, especially since they appear best suited for those who are mature and academically well prepared." Competency-based models let students move through material independently, advancing upon demonstrating content mastery, so they demand self-direction. The recommendation frames CBE as a complement to, not a replacement for, other course formats in community colleges.
requirements: Students need the maturity and academic preparation to move through material independently, advancing when they demonstrate content mastery.
constraints: The evaluation found CBE appears best suited for students who are mature and academically well prepared.
target_learners: community college students in online information technology programs
target_learning_goals: content mastery in career-relevant information technology programs of study
examples: The evaluation of online competency-based information technology programs at three community colleges informed this recommendation.

article_title: The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools
citation: Zohal Shah, Marilys Galindo, Chioma Aso-Hernandez, Christina Luke Luna, Keun-woo Lee, Josh Weisgrau, Teresa Solorzano, Britney Jacobs. (2024). The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Competency-Based Education with its seven elements of instructional practice
description: Competency-based education (CBE) is an education model that recognizes and accredits learners for demonstration of their skills and competencies instead of seat-time. The report adopts the Aurora Institute definition providing "seven critical elements of instructional practice," spanning learner decision-making, meaningful assessment, differentiated support, mastery-based progression, varied pathways and pacing, embedded equity strategies, and transparent common expectations. The report uses this framework to ground its argument that CBE is more adaptable to nonlinear learner pathways than seat-time credentialing.
requirements: Students must demonstrate mastery prior to advancing
Formative assessments integrated to inform daily instruction
Teachers communicate learning expectations with consistent assessment methods
constraints: Systematic implementation in K-12 is relatively new; policies limiting graduation-requirement flexibility can be barriers
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly historically and systematically excluded youth
target_learning_goals: Demonstration of competencies and skills across disciplines
examples: The Chugach School District in Alaska implemented CBE for over 20 years, replacing letter grades with emerging, developing, proficient, and advanced terminology and building a customized information management system.

citation: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Professional learning questionnaire characterizing curriculum-based professional learning across districts and schools
description: A questionnaire gathering information on professional learning in each district and its schools, grounded in a definition of curriculum-based professional learning (CBPL) as learning that supports implementation and sustained use of specific curriculum with integrity to the design while adapting to student needs. It includes four sections: basic district facts including built-in professional learning hours; types of professional learning structures such as PLCs and summer institutes with average monthly time; alignment with "11 CBPL features, including whether it is individualized or student focused"; and ratings of CBPL and HQIM implementation for each school. It is designed to identify best practices in districts where implementation is going well.

citation: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618
title: RDF/OWL/SKOS intervention-plan vocabulary with SHACL constraint layer
description: A lightweight RDF vocabulary, using the prefix cbe: within a competency-based education ontology extended for recourse representation, centered on the classes cbe:ActionPlan and cbe:Action. A plan is linked to actions via cbe:hasAction and to student and assessment via cbe:forStudent and cbe:forAssessment; SKOS provides "a controlled and extensible classification of activity types" such as quiz practice, forum participation, or resource review. SHACL shapes enforce timing (snapshotDay <= from <= to <= dueDay), budget (sum of action costs <= budget), and optional availability constraints, making plans machine-readable and checkable.

Activity types need known availability windows for the optional availability constraint
constraints: The current action vocabulary is described as necessarily simplified and derived from structured learner activity signals rather than richer pedagogical interaction data

examples: Listing 1 prints the ActionPlanShape and ActionShape requirements and SPARQL constraints C1-C3; Table I lists intervention features such as review quizzes and attend support with costs and constraints

article_title: Effect of classroom-based physical activity interventions on attention and on-task behavior in schoolchildren: A systematic review
citation: Ruhland Stefanie, Lange Klaus W. (2021). Effect of classroom-based physical activity interventions on attention and on-task behavior in schoolchildren: A systematic review. Sports Medicine and Health Science. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smhs.2021.08.003
title: Classroom-based physical activity (CB-PA) as physical activity during regular class time, inside or outside the classroom, excluding recess and lunch
description: The review defines CB-PA, following Watson and colleagues, as "PA during regular class time, which can occur either inside or outside the classroom, and which does not include time during school recess or lunch breaks." The construct covers two forms: short units of PA during breaks from lessons, and movement-enriched tuition in which PA mediates curriculum content (e.g., learning multiplication tables via invisible jump rope in TAKE 10!). Interventions may be performed with or without additional equipment, and intensity is mostly moderate to vigorous physical activity.
requirements: PA occurs during regular class time, not during recess or lunch breaks
constraints: Excludes time during school recess or lunch breaks; the review excluded studies of children with behavioral disorders such as ADHD or obesity
target_learners: school-aged children and adolescents aged 4–18 years
target_learning_goals: attention (selective, sustained, divided) and on-task behavior in the classroom
examples: TAKE 10! students learn multiplication tables by performing invisible jump rope; FUNtervals use 20 s high-intensity activity separated by 10 s rest repeated 8 times per day

article_title: Instructional design frameworks and intercultural models
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: CBM ID-TABLET: a management and design system of eight component areas
description: The ID-TABLET is CBM's management and design system, organizing the model into component areas covered across Chapters IV-XIV. These include CBM Inquiry (a monitoring system for the design process), Development (problem solving), Team (decision making), Assessments (forms of evaluation), Brainstorming (primary planning), Learners (instructional goals), Elements (content development across eight chapters), and Training (education about the product). The preface states that "the areas are ordered according to CBM's management and design system—the ID-TABLET," and Section II is designed to be used as a workbook with guiding questions for generic and specialized products.
requirements: Used as a handbook or reference resource; designers selectively attend to only those elements pertinent to a given project
constraints: Given the comprehensiveness of CBM's ID-TABLET, its areas are covered over several chapters; the problem for students may be limiting the number of design factors, given the amount of options offered in CBM
target_learners: students working alone or in small groups
target_learning_goals: Managing and designing culture-based ICT projects from inquiry through training
examples: Chapter XVI presents CBM Guide—Video Game Entries: Preproduction, illustrating an Add-on to an existing video game

article_title: Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors
citation: Antonija Mitrovic & Pramuditha Suraweera. (2016). Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:448–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0084-6
title: Constraint-Based Modeling with ideal solutions for tutoring ill-defined design tasks
description: The article describes the constraint-based approach used by KERMIT and EER-Tutor for teaching conceptual database design, an ill-defined task with huge solution spaces. Instead of requiring a problem solver, the tutor checks whether the student's schema is correct by matching it to constraints and a pre-specified ideal solution: "The ideal solution captures the semantics of the problem without the need for a problem solver". Syntactic constraints check ER-model syntax while semantic constraints compare the solution to the problem requirements, recognizing alternative correct solutions by looking for equivalent ways of specifying ER components.
requirements: A pre-specified ideal solution per problem, supplied by the human teacher
A constraint set distinguishing syntactic and semantic constraints
constraints: KERMIT stored only one correct solution per problem, although several correct solutions may exist for all but the simplest problems
target_learners: university students in introductory relational database courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design using the ER/EER models
examples: KERMIT matched submitted solutions to a constraint set of 92 constraints plus the ideal solution; EER-Tutor contains 57 problems and over 200 constraints

article_title: Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity
citation: Hyeonjin Kim and Michael J. Hannafin. (2008). Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-9010-9
title: Case-based reasoning (CBR) theory as an account of how expertise emerges through experience
description: CBR theory posits that individuals think, reason, and act based on experiences stored as cases. When facing a problem, people retrieve prior cases considered relevant to the new situation, generate a first-approximation solution, and evaluate results. Personal case libraries are indexed, which serves to structure individual case knowledge. The article uses CBR as the grounding theory for designing case-based activity learning environments.
requirements: Learners need access to exemplary expert cases because novices lack their own case knowledge
constraints: The article notes few longitudinal studies exist on how novices become experts through CBA or CBR approaches
examples: Chess experts retrieving memories of chess positions and appropriate playing methods

article_title: Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity
citation: Hyeonjin Kim and Michael J. Hannafin. (2008). Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-9010-9
title: Case-based activity (CBA) five-phase activity structure
description: CBA is an instructional pattern consisting of five phases: scenario work, what's the story, planning, doing, and telling your story. Scenario work establishes task context; what's the story supports analysis of expert cases; planning involves situation assessment and first-approximation solutions; doing is reflective action on plans; and telling your story supports reflection and transfer through constructing and sharing stories. The phases are designed to scaffold novices through authentic tasks with expert case support.
requirements: Access to expert case libraries
Instructor support and peer review
constraints: Novices tend to develop superficial scenarios without scaffolding
examples: A web-enhanced CBA course for preservice teachers learning to teach with technology, structured from a simple graphing program to WebQuest lesson planning

title: Pharmacy courses suited to CBL over LBL require integrating theory with practice in complex, context-dependent scenarios
description: The review identifies course characteristics that make pharmacy courses suitable for CBL rather than LBL: courses that "require more than rote memorization, requiring students to integrate theoretical knowledge with practical application, navigate complex, context-dependent scenarios, and develop problem-solving and clinical reasoning skills." Examples the article names include Clinical Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacognosy, Clinical Pharmacology, and clinical pharmacy practicums, all emphasizing application of knowledge to real or simulated patient cases. The pattern links course type to CBL's strengths in contextualized, interactive learning.

article_title: Application of case-based learning in psychology teaching: a meta-analysis.
citation: Wu Fanghui, Wang Tao, Yin Danxu, Xu Xiaoxiao, Jin Cancan, Mu Nan, Tan Qingrong. (2023). Application of case-based learning in psychology teaching: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04525-5
title: Case-based learning as a student-centered pedagogy distinguished from problem-based learning by prior-knowledge use and teacher guidance
description: The article characterizes CBL as "a student-centered pedagogy that requires students’ active participation in analyzing and discussing cases provided by the teacher", aiming to prepare students for professional practice by applying theoretical knowledge to contextual situations. Cases must be relevant, realistic, engaging, challenging, and instructional, with group case discussion as the core process. The article distinguishes CBL from PBL: CBL requires prior knowledge and trained-teacher guidance, whereas PBL involves solving problems with little previous knowledge and less teacher control, producing more "unfocused tangents".
requirements: Authentic and effective teaching cases are described as the key content, with achievement largely depending on case construction and facilitation
Inquiry-based learning, most commonly group discussion, is regarded as the instruction process for CBL
constraints: The article notes no standardized definition of CBL has been acknowledged
Applying CBL brings challenges and higher expectations to both teachers and students

target_learning_goals: applying theoretical knowledge to contextual situations
examples: Included trials implemented CBL alone or combined with simulated teaching, team-based learning, PBL, or flipped classroom formats across medical, nursing, management, experimental, and introductory psychology courses

The article describes an implementation sequence: "establishment of the case → case grouping and analysis → brainstorming → identifying instruction goals → new findings → exchanging results between groups → reaching learning consensus and integrating the consensus into clinical practice". title: CBC Behavioral Strategies Toolkit
description: The CBC Behavioral Strategies Toolkit (Sheridan et al., 2013), "consisting of 80 different intervention strategies, was used to standardize plan tactics in CBC casework."
